text: 🇲🇽⚖️ Mexico still wants answers on how "El Mayo" was taken to the United States. Sheinbaum assigned the federal Attorney General's Office to investigate the circumstances of his detention and transfer. — President Claudia Sheinbaum, mañanera, July 16 A capo delivered onto US soil outside any extradition process remains, for Mexico, a violation of its sovereignty to be accounted for.

🇲🇽🌱 From concrete to wetlands: rethinking how a nation heals its water. Mexico's river cleanup replaces "gray infrastructure" with natural solutions — wetlands, revegetation, reforested hillsides. Diagnostics covered 340 km and 322 sampling sites, exposing 3,202 industrial discharges and 479 clandestine dumps. — Alicia Bárcena, Environment Secretary, mañanera, July 16 Reconnecting people with living rivers is one of the program's four stated goals.

🇲🇽🔍 Sheinbaum wants independent international experts back on the Ayotzinapa case. In talks with the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, she proposed an independent expert group to review the methodology and validate new lines of investigation into the 43 disappeared students. — President Claudia Sheinbaum, mañanera, July 16 Nearly twelve years on, the state is inviting outside scrutiny — not hiding from it.

🇲🇽🛢️ Gas held at 24 pesos, diesel at 27 — even if global oil markets spike. Sheinbaum said the government will absorb international price shocks to keep fuel affordable for working families. — President Claudia Sheinbaum, mañanera, July 16 A sovereign energy policy means prices set in Mexico City, not by speculation on foreign markets.

🔥🇲🇽 89 textile factories caught dumping chemicals into Mexico's rivers. Eight shut down. Environmental inspectors hit polluting industries with fines of up to 56 million pesos and closed eight facilities outright. — Mañanera, July 16 Under the old model, industry poisoned the water and paid nothing. That era is ending.

🇲🇽🌊 20 billion pesos to bring three dead rivers back to life. Mexico is restoring the Atoyac, Lerma-Santiago and Tula — its three most contaminated rivers — reaching 25 million people across 10 states and 61 municipalities. — Alicia Bárcena, Environment Secretary, mañanera, July 16 The approach: nature-based solutions over concrete. 4,639 hectares restored, 4,667 tons of trash removed, 40,000 people in cleanup drives.

🚨🇲🇽 "Migration must not be persecuted." "If someone has committed a crime, they should be prosecuted — but migration is not a crime." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, mañanera, July 16 She was rejecting a US proposal to reactivate immigration detentions during routine traffic stops. The line is deliberate: Mexico refuses to treat migrants as criminals to be hunted at roadside checkpoints.

🇲🇽📈 MEXICAN HOUSEHOLDS KEEP SPENDING — 15 STRAIGHT MONTHS OF GROWTH

INEGI's flash consumption indicator shows private consumption rose 2.8% year-on-year in May and 2.6% in June, a 1.1% quarterly gain that reverses the first-quarter dip — 15 consecutive months of expansion. El Financiero names the driver plainly: record-low unemployment and real wages still climbing as inflation cools, keeping household purchasing power intact. That's what a "failing economy" looks like from the inside.

🇲🇽🇨🇺 AID SHIP FOR CUBA'S CHILDREN MAKES ITS LAST STOP IN CANCÚN

The Open Arms humanitarian ship docked in Cancún for its final stop before crossing to Havana, carrying medical supplies and 110 solar panels for the Juan Manuel Márquez pediatric hospital — a €165,000 solidarity campaign funded by more than 4,000 small donors. Blocked at five European ports before Mexico let it through, organizers called the US embargo on Cuba an "authentic medieval siege." "If we save one life," said Óscar Camps, "all of this will have been worthwhile."

🇲🇽🌎 MEXICO'S FUTURE DOESN'T DEPEND ON T-MEC

T-MEC renegotiation opens July 20, and Contralínea makes the point Washington won't want to hear: "If T-MEC disappeared in the next 10 years, it would mark the end of the economic liberalization project — but not necessarily Mexico's national development project." Analyst Carolina Hernández Calvario notes Mexico's fastest growth came when it protected strategic sectors and built its domestic market, not when it opened everything to the north.
